content: 1. The balance of desirable and undesirable effects of a 3-drug treatment regimen in patients with paucibacillary (PB) leprosy appears to favor the intervention, as the clinical benefits outweigh the potential harms. 2. The resource requirements for implementing a 3-drug regimen are moderate. While the cost of the 3-drug regimen is higher for PB patients, the cost of a 6-month regimen is lower for multibacillary (MB) patients compared to current regimens. Simplified logistics of using the same 3-drug combination for all leprosy patients may reduce costs for the pharmaceutical company providing the drugs. 3. Multidrug therapy (MDT) is provided free of charge to patients under an agreement with a pharmaceutical company. The cost of producing a 3-drug combination is unlikely to be significantly higher than producing two separate combinations. 4. There is no research evidence available to assess the certainty of resource requirements. However, if the pharmaceutical company increases the availability of MB-MDT (3-drug combination), there might be no additional costs for health programs. 5. The cost-effectiveness of the intervention is difficult to estimate due to limited clinical outcome data and varying effects across different patient groups. Costs of follow-up examinations also need to be considered. 6. Reducing the length of MB treatment is likely to improve compliance and reduce the need for frequent visits to healthcare facilities. This could enhance health equity by reducing costs associated with relapses and reactions in PB leprosy. 7. Stakeholders may be hesitant to adopt a shorter regimen due to the historical long-term treatment of leprosy and the slow resolution of lesions, which makes clinical improvement difficult to assess. 8. Implementation of a uniform multidrug therapy (UMDT) may be easier as it eliminates the need for accurate classification of leprosy into PB or MB at the primary healthcare level. This could reduce costs for both the health system and patients. 9. Training of healthcare workers would still be necessary to ensure proper implementation of the new treatment regimen. Standardized health education materials should be developed to support adherence to the new recommendations. 10. Monitoring compliance among PB patients after switching from a 2-drug to a 3-drug regimen is essential. Pharmacovigilance systems should be in place to monitor adverse events. 11. Research priorities include developing tools for bacteriological testing to monitor treatment outcomes, differentiating relapse from persistence of lesion activity, and studying the immunological aspects of neuritis and clinical management of reactions to reduce disability progression during and after antibiotic treatment. 12. For patients with rifampicin resistance, the recommended treatment involves at least two second-line drugs (clarithromycin, minocycline, or ofloxacin/levofloxacin/moxifloxacin) plus clofazimine daily for 6 months, followed by clofazimine and one of these drugs daily for an additional 18 months. If ofloxacin resistance is also present, ofloxacin and its derivatives should not be used. 13. Molecular testing for resistance can guide the selection of second-line regimens. However, implementation of second-line regimens may be challenging due to higher costs and longer treatment durations. 14. Data on resistance trends and second-line treatment outcomes should be expanded and monitored as per the guidance in the WHO’s 2017 update on antimicrobial resistance surveillance in leprosy.
